title: Decode a real function call by hand
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read the machine code of a function call, say which registers carry what, and explain why a function that calls nothing needs no stack frame.

blocks.text: Nothing in the instruction set says where arguments go or how a function returns. That is an agreement, not a rule — a calling convention, agreed between compilers so that code compiled separately can be linked together. Once you can read it, generated code stops being opaque.

rows: Nobody — the caller assumes they are destroyed
The callee, if it calls anything
The caller, if it needs them after the call

blocks.title: Two save categories exist because both choices are sometimes right
blocks.text: If every register were caller-saved, a function making many calls would save constantly. If every register were callee-saved, a small function would save registers it barely touches. Splitting the set lets a compiler put short-lived values in scratch registers and long-lived ones in preserved registers, and pay for saving only what is actually needed. Reading which category a value lands in tells you what the compiler concluded about its lifetime.

blocks.caption: Generated aarch64 for a function that calls another
lines: int caller(int x) {
int r = helper(x, x + 1, x + 2);
return r * 2;
_caller:
stp  x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!    ; push frame pointer and return address
mov  x29, sp                  ; establish this frame
add  w1, w0, #1               ; second argument   = x + 1
add  w2, w0, #2               ; third argument    = x + 2
; first argument is already in w0
bl   _helper                  ; call: jump, and save the return address
lsl  w0, w0, #1               ; result arrives in w0; multiply by 2
ldp  x29, x30, [sp], #16      ; restore, and pop the frame
ret                           ; jump to the saved return address

items: Arguments are placed in numbered registers in order, and x is already in the first one
The call instruction both jumps and records where to come back to
The return value arrives in the same register the first argument used
The return address must be saved because the call inside will overwrite it
The frame is popped in one instruction that also restores both saved registers

blocks.caption: The same compiler, a leaf function
lines: int leaf(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
_leaf:
add  w0, w1, w0
ret
/* Two instructions. No stack frame at all. */

blocks.title: This is the clearest evidence of what a stack frame is for
blocks.text: This particular trivial leaf needs no frame: it makes no call and has no spills, address-taken locals, variable-length objects or alignment work. Other leaf functions can still need a frame for those reasons. Inlining may remove call and frame overhead when the remaining function body no longer needs stack storage.

blocks.caption: The layout, from the stack pointer upward
lines: higher addresses
...caller's frame...
| saved return addr |   only if this function calls anything
| saved frame ptr   |
| callee-saved regs |   only those actually used
| local variables   |   those that need an address, or were spilled
| outgoing args     |   beyond what fits in registers
lower addresses
/* This is the layout the operating systems course's backtraces walk,
and the structure the C course's stack-lifetime bugs corrupt. */

items: A debugger walks these frames to produce a backtrace — the same backtrace the deadlock lesson used
A buffer overflow that reaches the saved return address changes where the function returns to, which is the mechanism the C course described
Protections such as stack canaries and shadow stacks exist specifically to defend this structure
Reading a frame tells you what a function is holding and why, including values that appear in no source line

blocks.title: Read the convention off your own compiler
steps: Write a function taking three arguments that calls another function, and compile with -O1 -S
Identify which register each argument was placed in, and where the return value arrives
Write a leaf function and confirm it has no stack frame at all
Add a call to the leaf function and watch the frame appear
Write a function with more arguments than fit in registers and find where the extras go
Compile with -O2 and check whether the small function was inlined instead of called
Run the program under a debugger, break inside the inner function, and print a backtrace
Match each line of that backtrace to a saved return address on the stack
blocks.expected: Argument registers identified by reading real output, a leaf function with no frame, and a frame that appears the moment you add a call. The debugger step ties it together: the backtrace you have used in earlier courses is nothing more than a walk over the saved return addresses you just watched being written.

cheatsheet: The calling convention is an agreement between compilers, not part of the ISA
The first several registers carry arguments; the return value comes back in the first
The call instruction jumps and saves the return address in a link register
Caller-saved registers are scratch; callee-saved must be preserved if used
Two categories exist so short-lived and long-lived values can each be cheap
A function that calls nothing needs no frame — verified: a leaf compiled to two instructions
The frame exists because of the call inside it, which is why inlining removes it
The frame holds the saved return address, saved registers, locals and extra arguments
A backtrace is a walk over saved return addresses; overflow attacks target the same field

checkpoint.prompt: A leaf function compiles to two instructions with no stack frame. Why does it need none?

choices.A: It calls nothing, so nothing will overwrite its return address
choices.B: Leaf functions use a separate stack
choices.C: The compiler optimised the whole frame away in this particular build

checkpoint.explanation: Verified: the same compiler produced a full frame for a function containing a call and none for one without. The frame exists because of the call, which is also why inlining removes it.

checkpoint.prompt: Why do calling conventions define both caller-saved and callee-saved registers?

choices.A: Because some registers are faster, so compilers favour them
choices.D: So each function saves only what it actually needs

checkpoint.explanation: One category alone forces unnecessary saving in one direction or the other. Which category a value lands in tells you what the compiler concluded about its lifetime. Short-lived values use scratch registers and long-lived ones preserved registers, which is what lets each function save only what it needs.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the call instruction do beyond jumping?

choices.D: It saves the flags to the stack as well

checkpoint.explanation: The callee knows where to come back to. The callee then saves that address to the stack only if it makes a call of its own, which is precisely the difference between a leaf function and one that is not.

checkpoint.prompt: How does a debugger produce a backtrace?

choices.A: It walks the stack frames, reading each saved return address
choices.B: The kernel records every call in a trace the debugger can read
choices.C: It reads a log the program wrote

checkpoint.explanation: It is the same structure a buffer overflow corrupts when it reaches the saved return address — which is why the protections around that field exist.

checkpoint.prompt: In the shown AArch64 caller, which register already holds the first integer argument?
checkpoint.explanation: The caller receives x in w0. It computes the second and third arguments into w1 and w2 before bl helper.

checkpoint.prompt: Which instruction in the example transfers control to helper and records where to return?
checkpoint.explanation: bl branches to the callee and writes the return address to the link register. Saving that value to the stack is separate work.

checkpoint.prompt: After helper returns, where does the shown caller find its integer result?
checkpoint.explanation: The example shifts w0 immediately after bl helper. Under this lesson’s AArch64 example, w0 carries the returned integer value.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does caller save x30 before it calls helper?

choices.A: It needs an extra argument register
choices.B: A nested call would replace caller’s return address
choices.D: The stack requires every function to save x30

checkpoint.explanation: bl helper writes a new return address to x30. caller must preserve its own return address before that overwrite if it will later return.

checkpoint.prompt: What does stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]! do in the shown prologue?

choices.A: Restores two registers and raises sp
choices.B: Saves the frame pointer and return address while allocating 16 bytes

checkpoint.explanation: The paired store writes x29 and x30 at the decremented stack pointer. The ! updates sp as part of that instruction.

checkpoint.prompt: Which statement about callee-saved registers is correct?

choices.B: The caller may always discard its value after a call
choices.C: They are only used by leaf functions
choices.D: A callee that uses one must restore its incoming value before returning

checkpoint.explanation: Callee-saved means the called function preserves the value visible to its caller when it chooses to use that register.

checkpoint.prompt: Which fact can make a compiler create a frame even for a function that does not call another function?

choices.A: Its local state needs stack storage, such as an addressable or spilled value

checkpoint.explanation: The two-instruction leaf is one observed example, not a universal promise. Locals, spills, alignment, or tool settings can still require stack space.

checkpoint.prompt: What does ldp x29, x30, [sp], #16 accomplish before ret?

choices.C: Restores saved state and releases this 16-byte frame

checkpoint.explanation: The paired load restores x29 and x30 from the current stack frame, then post-indexing raises sp by 16 bytes.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a calling convention needed when both caller and callee are compiled separately?

choices.A: It makes all functions use the same instruction count
choices.B: It chooses a cache replacement policy
choices.D: It lets code agree on argument, result, and preservation locations

checkpoint.explanation: Separate pieces of machine code need a shared contract for where values go and which registers survive a call.

checkpoint.prompt: A debugger follows saved return addresses to show a backtrace. Which field is it using in the shown non-leaf frame?
checkpoint.explanation: The return address saved from x30 links this frame to the instruction that resumes in its caller, allowing stack walking.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can inlining remove call-frame work in an appropriate build?

choices.A: It changes all locals into globals
choices.B: The call site disappears, so no nested call needs its return address preserved
choices.D: It turns every function into a system call

checkpoint.explanation: When the compiler replaces a call with the callee body, there may be no call instruction and no nested return address to save at that call site.
